rows.note: Single typed `payment_amount` (int minor units); no amount summing. AmountRange.max enforced; over-cap rejected. Cancellation has no field to cancel.

AllowedPayee matches on Merchant.id (required field); a wrong id is rejected even with a matching display name. No alphabetical/decoy-key target derivation (contrast ASU RT-2/RT-3). The id is what is bound.

SAMPLE renderer only. The constraint check was executed; the card's display logic was read from MandateCard.tsx source (not rendered in a browser). Constraints bind Merchant.id, but the web-client MandateCard summarises `payee.name` (agent/merchant-chosen) with no length cap or invisible-char handling. A human reading the card sees a name that is not the bound identifier -> distinct effects (ids) can share a display name. Spec relies on a 'trusted surface'; this is a sample weakness, not the signed binding.

Pre-set payee in the open mandate is enforced (check_preset_payment_claims); currency mismatch rejected by AmountRange. The grant cannot be stretched to another payee or currency at the constraint layer.

Budget is cumulative ONLY via a caller-supplied MandateContext.total_amount; the SDK does not persist or accumulate it. Without context it fails closed (fails_closed=True). But if the integrator does not persist and accumulate usage across uses, two sub-budget payments both pass (split_works=True): aggregate 2008c exceeds the 2007c budget. Argument-level: depends on integrator state, not a break of the signed mandate.
No AP2-provided trusted renderer; card text handling is client/surface side (see AB6).
No agent-named label surface in the signed mandate; fields are typed models.
Enrollment/credential registration is out of scope of the mandate SDK (holder keys are provisioned by the issuer/device).
Mandate binding is a signed SD-JWT over structured payloads, not a concatenated challenge; JCS/sd_hash are injective within the SDK.
The user's device signs the mandate; the renderer (surface) does not choose the signed bytes. Sample couples assemble+sign in an agent tool (noted in AB6).
Closed mandate is signed; substituting a different closed mandate breaks the holder signature / constraint check (equivalent to AB3). No separate post-approval window.
No volume/approval-prompt primitive in the SDK; flooding is a surface/UX concern.
validate_for_execution rebinds to current_action_digest; substitution -> action_digest_mismatch. Consume-once enforced.
ActionBinding.to_canonical hashes the entire parameters mapping + target; there is no alphabetical/decoy target derivation. Any extra/renamed field changes the digest -> digest mismatch at execution.
No amount heuristic or summing; amount is just a bound parameter. Changing it changes the digest.

The approval_protocol module imposes no per-agent rate limit or pending-cap; 50 requests open freely. Impact is bounded because only an AUTHENTICATED human/role entry can resolve a request (advisory LLM cannot, see AB5), so this is push-bombing of the human, not an auto-approve. ADR-0030 does not claim flood control; rate limiting is left to the host.

LLM_ADVISORY entries are recorded but never satisfy a stage (ADR-0030 s8); advisory-only -> no_resolution. An unverified/self-asserted approver cannot satisfy a stage either (stage.authorizes by identity/role).

Executed. The digest is SHA-256 over RFC 8785 JCS of a structured object. Within the Python SDK it is injective on our cases (distinct digests: True); there is no concatenation. Documented gap (ADR-0030 step 6): floats use CPython repr, so 3 of 5 sample floats serialise differently from RFC 8785/ECMAScript (1e+21, 1e-06, 1e-07). A non-Python verifier could compute a different digest for the same float. That is a parity failure, which fails closed, not a collision inside one SDK. The authors track it as parity work.
No delegated grant/'allow similar' primitive in the protocol module; each action is a fresh binding. Nothing to stretch.
No renderer in the module; the human-facing card is produced by host handlers (callback/console/webhook). Padding/bidi handling is handler-dependent and out of the security contract tested here.

The binding digest is over the full action; display injectivity depends on the host handler, not this module. The ADR explicitly rejects trusting a self-asserted approver name (does not claim trusted rendering).
Approver identities/roles are configured in the ApprovalChain; there is no open enrollment of approving credentials in this module.
The execution boundary recomputes the digest independently of any renderer, so the rendering party does not choose the signed bytes at this layer.
No aggregate/threshold limit primitive; that is a policy-layer concern above ADR-0030.

blank-glyph/bidi padding (executed, in-memory MCP session): A 521-character message with 400x U+2800, U+202E and 50x U+3164 padding reached the client's elicitation_callback byte-for-byte (no escape, collapse or length cap). The SDK forwards the server-authored `message` unchanged and binds the answer to no effect. The MCP spec leaves display to the client, so this is an SDK-layer observation. A client that sanitises the message and shows which server is asking, or URL mode, mitigates it. In our threat model the text reaching the human is attacker-influenced.

label spoofing in prompt text (executed, in-memory MCP session): Server text imitating trusted labels ('Verified by client: YES', 'Target: ...') reached the client verbatim, while the tool ran with a different payee. The SDK forwards the server-authored `message` unchanged and binds the answer to no effect. The MCP spec leaves display to the client, so this is an SDK-layer observation. A client that sanitises the message and shows which server is asking, or URL mode, mitigates it. In our threat model the text reaching the human is attacker-influenced.

non-injective rendering (executed, in-memory MCP session): Two different effects (10 to acct-utility-001; 10000 to acct-placeholder-999) produced byte-identical elicitation requests (message + schema), and both executed after 'accept'. The SDK forwards the server-authored `message` unchanged and binds the answer to no effect. The MCP spec leaves display to the client, so this is an SDK-layer observation. A client that sanitises the message and shows which server is asking, or URL mode, mitigates it. In our threat model the text reaching the human is attacker-influenced.

Form-mode results are returned to the server via the client and are not cryptographically bound to any tool-effect digest, so a compromised client/agent can alter or synthesise the 'accept' content (docstring even says an agent client 'might ... automatically generat[e] a response'; our executed run's callback synthesises 'accept' in code and the tool runs). URL mode keeps the interaction out of band (stronger for P1/P4). No effect-binding either way.
Elicitation collects typed form fields; it is not an amount-bearing approval of a specific effect.
No recipient/target binding: elicitation is a generic prompt, not an effect descriptor.
No delegated grant primitive.
No credential enrollment in the elicitation surface.
No concatenated challenge; form schema is validated JSON-Schema (injective).
URL mode deliberately moves the ceremony off the client; form mode has no signed bytes.
No volume/rate primitive in the elicitation API (host concern).
No aggregate-limit primitive.

STATIC. exec-approval card runs sanitizeExecApprovalDisplayText: invisible-char escaping, length cap (oversized marker), and secret redaction, with a stripped-view bypass check. This is exactly the escape/collapse/cap that ASU's RT-5 flags as MISSING in ASU pre-fix — a fair positive contrast.

STATIC. allow-always exec grants are keyed to the resolved argv (+cwd), so a different command/argv needs fresh approval (audit: P2 PASS).
